The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly
positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who
are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique
form factor. We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display
on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues
with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for
a replacement.
The company says the problem affects a very small number of iPhone
Duo units and appears to surface relatively quickly. Most iPhone
Duo units are not affected. You do not need AppleCare+ to have
your iPhone Duo replaced for this problem. If you bought from a
carrier, you should contact AppleCare directly, not your carrier,
to get your device replaced.
Did it cross Ternus’s mind to just say “You’re folding it wrong?”
(History doesn’t repeat, and in this case, it actually doesn’t even rhyme. Steve Jobs never told anyone they were “holding it wrong” with the iPhone 4 — he emailed a customer, “Just avoid holding it in that way.” But CNN went with the headline “Apple on iPhone Complaints: You’re Holding It Wrong” and that’s the line everyone wrongly remembers.)

articles.title: MTL-style circuit simulator
articles.summary:
After the first attempt at making a very side-effectful circuit simulator, and
then an ambitious attempt at making it pure, I was reminded of a middle ground,
using a pattern common in production Haskell code. It is called MTL-style
effects, and it is a specific type of final tagless encoding.





The idea is that we first find a set of operations that our circuit simulator
needs to support. Drawing this boundary well requires some experience and taste.
Then we encode that limited set of operations into a type class. Here’s one way
to do it.




In[1]:
class CircuitOperations m where
 make_wire :: m Wire
 get_signal :: Wire -> m Signal
 set_signal :: Wire -> Signal -> m ()
 add_action :: Wire -> m () -> m ()
 after_delay :: Int -> m () -> m ()
 get_time :: m Int
 probe_output :: String -> m ()
 propagate :: m ()

(Continue reading the full article on the web.)

articles.title: What’s Left for ‘Pro and Tell’ Week: Touch-Enabled OLED MacBooks
articles.summary:
Joe Rossignol, MacRumors:
Apple on Wednesday will announce 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro
models featuring touch-enabled OLED displays with thinner bezels,
a Dynamic Island instead of a notch, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, and
a lighter and slightly thinner design, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman
reports. Apple is hosting a private “Pro and tell” experience
in Los Angeles starting at 10 a.m. Pacific Time tomorrow.
I’m here in LA for the press shindig tomorrow. One thing I’ve been thinking about regarding these reported touch-enabled OLED MacBooks is that Gurman has reported for months that these new MacBooks will sport M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. Here’s Gurman back on June 26:
The MacBook models, positioned at the top of Apple’s lineup, will
arrive between late this year and early next year, according to
people with knowledge of the matter. They’re planned to be powered
by the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, said the people, who
asked not to be identified because the plans are private. [...]
The first touch-screen 14-inch and 16-inch models, code-named K114
and K116, will represent the biggest overhaul of Apple’s high-end
laptops since the company began moving away from Intel Corp. chips
in 2020. An Apple spokesperson declined to comment on the
company’s plans.
Apple’s decision to use the M5 line before jumping to a future M7
is part of a broader shift in its chip strategy. The company is
skipping M6-generation Pro and Max chips altogether, breaking from
its usual approach. Bloomberg News reported on this
strategy earlier this week.
If that’s all true, it’s certainly unusual for Apple to skip the Pro and Max variants for the M6 chip generation. But there have been oddities with the higher-end Apple Silicon chips before. (There was no M4 Ultra chip, for example, and the M3 Ultra didn’t appear until the March 2025 Mac Studio update, 18 months after the M3 generation debuted.) But what I would find downright weird is that the current MacBook Pros already sport the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. They came out in March. So what’s the idea here? That Apple replaces the current higher-end MacBook Pros with versions whose only upgrades are to the chassis and display, but the performance remains the same? That’s certainly possible, I guess, but it would be weird.
So I’m just wondering if tomorrow’s new touchscreen OLED MacBooks aren’t replacements for the current MacBook Pros, but instead are the start of a new MacBook family with another name. I don’t think they’d call them MacBook “Duos”, because they’re not two-in-one devices. MacBook “Ultras”, maybe — with the same specs as the MacBook Pros but more expensive displays? But “Ultra” seems like a wrong name for a MacBook because Apple’s M-series Ultra chips are (to date at least) desktop only. It’d be weird if the M5 Ultra is exclusive to the Mac Studio while the MacBook “Ultra” maxes out with the M5 Max. So maybe they just are the new MacBook Pros and this first OLED/touch generation uses the same chips as the ones from March?
That’s what I’m most curious about heading into tomorrow.
 ★

articles.title: Inches & Miles
articles.summary:
The AI era seems to be emboldening startups to once again take bold swings and use your data without even bothering to ask so they can build a startup around it.

It’s the great truism of the internet: You give an inch, and folks will take a mile.
Back when I was running ShortFormBlog in 2009, I remember trying a number of digital startups, all of which promised different ways to help monetize my content through optimization or some clever feature that made my site 5% better. These scripts were mostly horrible, with the exception of Apture, humane tech advocate Tristan Harris’ startup. I eventually got rid of most of them as I quickly realized what they were doing. But most of them had an underlying goal: They wanted my audience’s data.
The most notable example of this was Facebook’s Like button, perhaps the most infamous bait-and-switch conducted by the company before the pivot to video. The company convinced websites large and small to put a little code on their page in exchange for a chance at traffic. (And worse, they wouldn’t let you customize the damn thing to match the look of your site, so it looked ugly as sin.) But what was actually happening was two things: Facebook had created a massive dragnet of data on its users by making random websites a part of its network, and it was setting the stage for a lot of people to eventually shut down their external website and stay on Facebook. For better or worse, it changed online culture forever.
As silly as it sounds, those like buttons were spying on you back in 2010. All of them. (Quilia/Unsplash)
The external Like button died earlier this year, having served its purpose. Now, if you want to link your own website on one of those Facebook pages you quickly linked back to, you have to pay Facebook money. I’m not kidding.
I’ve been thinking a lot about this era, which brought us chumboxes and ever-intrusive ads, because it kind of feels like what’s starting to happen with AI.
Case in point: Over the weekend, I got an email from an AI company that wanted me to link their product. Not exactly unique these days. But what was unique was that it was essentially a form letter from a service called Listaify, which appeared to be a middleman that promised to get platforms to link your little startup.


This site exists to build up dofollow links for vibe-coded AI apps. I’m going to reward them by talking about them, but not linking them.
I did some research on this and what I found was that Listaify had put me on their site, informing audiences that I was “accepting AI tools.” Now, if you read my prior post about these AI-based submissions, you probably know that I was not exactly raring to promote every AI product under the sun. Much the opposite. But this company had gone out of its way to describe my posting habits, what I was willing to accept and not accept, and my apparent reach. (But apparently, they had missed the part where I got iLands to add unsubscribe links to their AI bots by drawing attention to their bad behavior.)
Put another way, this company scraped my data. That’s bad.
But here’s what’s worse: This company not only tries to shove links into my inbox at a time when a lot of companies are shoving links into my inbox, but it has turned it into a business. It essentially encourages startups to pay them hundreds or even thousands of dollars per year to help you promote your tools on various blogs and platforms.
This sucks—it is a systematic strategy to wear bloggers down to promote AI tools, even if it’s not their focus. Plus, by placing themselves in the middle of the relationship, they’re taking potential advertising revenue away from outlets that could use it. This is not why I got into blogging nearly 20 years ago, and it’s not why I’m going to do it now.
Services like these exploit founders and creators by attempting to optimize everything to within an inch of its life, and it does more harm to the ecosystem than help. This is not uncommon with PR pitches, but it feels like every decision I make, every word I write on my site is a data point for someone else to exploit readers.
If you use this service, at least when it comes to Tedium, you are wasting your money. (In fact I updated my contribute page to forbid it.) If you want to support independent journalism, don’t exploit it.
(I will note, to their credit, that when I complained, they removed me. But there was no apology, no recognition that their attempt to push even more AI projects into my inbox might be unwelcome.)
But they’re not the only example of take-an-inch-give-a-mile philosophy I’m seeing creep up in a big way. Recently, I recently got a series of LinkedIn messages from a person running an adtech platform. He informed me that he had gathered all my past sponsor info to fill his database and was willing to give me access to it for free. I felt uncomfortable about the fact that he just took my data and was essentially trying to offer it back to me, and so (after thinking it over for a while), I told him to remove my information from his platform. Despite being so desperate to get my attention previously, he never replied.
I understand the nature of scraping of public data. It can be done in responsible ways. (And yes, it’s likely that ) And scraping is probably going to be an important part of the future of the internet. But in both of these cases, companies I never heard of tried to insert themselves into my business. And in both cases, I had to point out that I had not given them permission to do so.
Companies like these take an inch and give a mile. And they’re far from alone. There’s no ethics to it. It’s take-an-inch-give-a-mile across the board. It’s what eventually leads people to stop giving inches.
The internet, ignoring the gatekeeping, was built on a collective sense of altruism. People helping out other people. It’s why Craigslist exists, after all. But it just takes a few bad actors to ruin the whole thing, which means that it was arguably spoiled long ago. And as these examples highlight, there are more bad actors than ever.
I have talked repeatedly about how much I hate gatekeeping. But this is the kind of crap that makes people put up gates. We’re already seeing it on Reddit, where moderators for r/opensource awkwardly tried banning AI projects, only to face massive backlash.
I don’t want the internet to be a gatekeepery scene again. But they’re making it hard.

articles.title: The upvote dilemma
articles.summary:
A couple of weeks ago I quietly removed the upvote count from the discovery feed on Bear. The upvote button is still there on every post, and upvotes still decide what ends up on Trending. You just can’t see the numbers next to each post anymore.
I made the change for two reasons.
The first is that visible counts make the popular posts more popular. A post with a lot of upvotes looks like it’s worth reading, so it gets read and upvoted more, and the quiet posts with no audience stay quiet. One of the things I love about Bear, and actively curate, is that someone with no audience can still be discovered. Hiding the count means people judge a post by its title and writing, not by how many people liked it first, especially on the Newest page.
The second is that upvote numbers don't make people feel good. Someone puts sincere effort into a post, publishes it, and then sees a little “1” next to it, sitting right below someone else’s “214”. Writing shouldn’t feel like a popularity contest, and a number next to your name makes it one, whether you like it or not.
More broadly, I think the "like button" is one of the things that made the internet worse (that and infinite scroll). It turned writing and sharing into a scoreboard, and it trained a generation of platforms (and people) to optimise for the number instead of the thing itself. I’ve been critical of this in my post on social media, and it felt a bit hypocritical to have the same mechanic on Bear’s own feed.
Despite my above grievances, upvotes are useful. They’re a good, simple signal to indicate what people have enjoyed, and I haven’t found a better way to rank the feed (yet). This feels like a decent tradeoff. Upvotes still do the useful job of ranking, but they no longer act as a public scoreboard.
I was a little worried making this change (hence the quiet rollout to test it), since part of the appeal of upvoting is seeing number go up. So I compared the two weeks after the change with the month prior, and the number of upvotes per day didn’t change, the number of people upvoting didn’t change, and neither did the number of people clicking through to posts from the feed. People are reading and upvoting as much as before. They’re just not comparing scores while they do it, and upvotes are spread out among more posts than before. Great success!
It’s still early days, and I’ll keep an eye on it over the next month. But for now the numbers are staying hidden.
If you have thoughts on this, send me an email. I’d love to hear how it feels from your side, both as a reader and as a writer.

articles.title: The NYT Seemingly Does Marissa Mayer Dirty
articles.summary:
Alexandra Alter, in the lede for her profile of Marissa Mayer’s new AI startup Dazzle for The New York Times (gift link):
Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like
an impossible task.
Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher
wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special.
Mayer — the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at
Google, where she was the first female engineer — likes cracking
a hard problem. But she felt overwhelmed by the range and
complexity of potential answers.
So Mayer asked her personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle. Within a few
seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer.
“It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative
and an animal lover,” Mayer said. She thought it was perfect.
That anecdote is brutal. It makes it seem like Mayer has lost her mind. She’s getting roasted for it on social media. I suspected (and hoped) there was more to the story. There was. Here’s Mayer herself on X:
To be clear, I didn’t use Dazzle because I was overwhelmed by
making a slide. I used it because summing up your child in a few
bullets feels laughably limiting. And, since our team had just
gotten an early prototype running, I wanted to see what deeper
threads it might find.
She might just be hyping her startup. But she definitely didn’t tell The Times that she needed help from AI to remember that her own daughter is “empathetic, creative, and an animal lover”. She seemingly got done dirty by Alter and the Times on that use-case anecdote.
 ★

articles.title: Pluralistic: History is something you do (27 Oct 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links History is something you do: Not something that happens to you. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Occupy Tents are speech; Piagram; SOPA; "I'm Rob Fucking Ford"; Blocking all porn in the UK; Pirates rule Iceland; Shake Shack v shitting to death. Upcoming appearances: Vienna, Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. History is something you do (permalink) Prediction is hard. Especially about the future. That Yogi Berra gem proves that you don't have to be a science fiction writer to get irritated with people insisting that you must know what's going to happen tomorrow, but (as a sf writer), I can tell you that this is one of our main occupational hazards. Obviously, this is a self-inflicted injury. Our genre is full of big names who self-mythologized as scientific Nostradamuses. From the "future history" bar-charts in Heinlein's books (I was once on a panel with Robert Silverberg where he referred to RAH as "Robert A Timeline") to the McGuffin of Asimov's Foundation series: a "scientific" discipline that could predict the trajectory of human civilization for millennia into the future. But me, I find the prospect of predicting the future incredibly dismal – even offensive. A predictable future is set in stone, immune to human agency. A predictable future runs on rails, and we're the prisoners of history, tied to the tracks. For me, the most exciting thing about sf is the idea that the future is contingent. Sf is a long, sharp pin that can prick inevitabilism's bubble: that assertion by tech-bros and policymakers alike that the future is out of our hands and must be accommodated, not shaped. Inevitabilism is a form of vulgar Thatcherism, the assertion that "there is no alternative." If The Market won't deliver an energy transition, and it leaves us to boil in our own skins, drown in the rising seas, and roast in wildfires, then tough shit humanity, there is no alternative. If there's a tech company eavesdropping on all of our communications technologies and following us as we move through digital and physical space (and turning the juiciest tidbits over the ICE), that's not the tech company's fault: there is no alternative. If some broadly useful statistical tools are delivered in the most climate-destroying, economy-wrecking, job-killing, quality-vaporizing way possible, that's just How It Is. It's not Sam Altman or Dario Amodei's fault: there is no alternative. Science fiction can do more than imagine how "General AI" might change society: sf can imagine a society that doesn't make the fanciful leap from a word-guessing sentence-extruder to a machine god. Sf can imagine a world that debuts "AI" as a joint supercomputing project between the IPCC and Sandia National Labs whose primary purpose is to improve the fidelity of climate models, and whose spinoffs are modest but interesting open source tools that people run on regular computers with normal energy footprints. Considered as a predictive literature, sf is a colossal failure. If our books are to be taken as roadmaps to an inevitable future, we have all flunked out of cartography school. More than 99.9% of these maps describe a territory that never emerged. All claims of sf's predictive value are just survivor bias, feats of Texas marksmanship in which we fire a shotgun into the side of a barn and then draw a target around the place where the holes cluster. What's more likely: that sf is 99.9% fake fortune-tellers and 0.1% seers and soothsayers; or that the "predictions that came true" in sf are just the inevitable bullseyes that you'd score if you threw enough darts? Prediction is a weak and helpless activity, the obsession of people who don't think they can change anything. It's the superstitious dread that gives rise to astrology. Far better to be a Luddite who asserts that there is more than one way to introduce a technology to a society. To be a Luddite is to insist that humans are in charge of humanity, not the iron laws of economics, not the great forces of history, not the uncaring and illusory constellations. At its best, sf is a proudly Luddite literature: https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-science-fiction-is-a-luddite-literature/ The insistence that we can change things is an active posture. It's an activist posture. At its radical best, sf is activist, because it engages with more than what the machine does, insisting on changing who the machine does it for and who the machine does it to. Which is why I find demands to offer predictions for the future so irritating. People who think that sf writers can predict the future have the field's role exactly backwards. My intention isn't to demoralize you into tying yourself to history's tracks – I'm here to show you how to grab the wheel and steer off the rails altogether. The reason this seems so implausible is that the "there is no alternative" people have convinced us that all change is the result of individuals. To change the world, you must fashion yourself into one of history's mediocre Great Men, a Musk or Zuck. Our oligarchs are the avatars of the Great Forces of History. They have seen the predictable, inevitable future and have been allocated trillions by the capital markets to ensure that we arrive there on time, running straight down those shining rails, no matter how many people are tied to the tracks. Another motif of Thatcherism (and hence inevitabilism) is that "there is no such thing as society," which means that all change is the result of individuals, which means that only Great Men can hope to change anything. If there is no such thing as society, then it follows that there's no such thing as mass movements, there's no such thing as trade unions, and there's no such thing as revolutions. If there's no such thing as society, then eruptions of students and workers in the streets must be nothing more than mob violence – it can't possibly be a political eruption. If you're an inevitabilist than Occupy was nothing more than millions of individual "virtue signallers" and #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter were the individual follies of innumerable "social justice warriors." As an activist, I'm not interested in predicting the future, I'm interested in changing it. When I speak about "the post-American internet" that we could create by exploiting the policy space that has been opened by Trump's incontinent belligerence, my intention is to get you to help build it, not to get you to prepare yourself for that inevitable outcome: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition Obviously, some aspects of our future are locked in. The climate violence our political and business elites inflicted on the world locked in rising seas, extreme weather, habitat-loss driven zoonotic plagues and massive refugee crises. Those are inevitable. What's entirely up to us is what we do about them. Do we create full employment for every person who will live for the next 300 years, relocating our coastal cities inland, treating the sick, retrofitting our infrastructure, and accommodating our neighbors who are driven out of their homes? Or do we let the stupidest, worst people among us lead us into the ecofascism of border walls, drone warfare, and exterminationism? That's our choice. We've had generations of being told to "vote with our wallets" instead of organizing in political, labor and social movements. Voting with your wallet doesn't work (billionaires' wallets are thicker than yours, they win those votes), and if you lose enough of those wallet elections, it's easy to fall into the despair of believing that the future is inevitable: https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/13/consumption-choices/#marginal-benefits I think this is why "prediction markets" have caught on so ferociously. While prediction markets are sold as a way for people to "inject information" into markets, they are actually a rigged system that transfers money from everyday "investors" to insiders: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/24/degenerated-gambling/#oracle-capture Prediction markets are the perfect pastime for history's prisoners. If you fancy yourself a plaything of the gods whose future is already written, then prediction markets are a way for you and your fellow prisoners to bet on what torments will come next. And of course oligarchs love prediction markets, because they're the ones who can rig the odds, say, by placing a bet on a war and then leading the country to that war. They are the gods, the only ones who get to make history, so a market for bets on what history will do next is a way to enrich history's avatars at the expense of history's victims. In science fiction, we often meet powerful aliens who tell us "resistance is futile" as they conquer our world and set about exterminating us. But if resistance was truly futile, no one would have to say it. When they tell us "there is no alternative," what they mean is "stop trying to think of alternatives." To imagine radically is to move beyond the helplessness of prediction: a radical imagination dares to insist that history is what we make, not what happens to us.
